1:
Robertson thinks it fitting that one of the angels who carried the bowls should explain a judgment already pronounced, and notes that the noun used is the same the Greek Old Testament uses of the doom of Babylon, the genitive marking it a judgment upon the harlot rather than one she passes. Gill asks which of the seven it was, reports that Brightman named the fifth because his vial fell on the seat of the beast, and prefers the seventh, as concerned in the final destruction. Wesley notices that this vision and the later one of the bride of the Lamb open in the same words, a token of the exact opposition between them. Barnes treats the chapter as an explanatory episode in which the action is delayed so that the power about to be judged may first be described. Clarke does something none of the others do. He declines to expound the chapter in his own person, prints instead the fullest exposition he has met with, tells his readers they are at perfect liberty to reject it, and closes by saying that God alone knows all the secrets of his own wisdom.

Who the woman is divides them more sharply than anything else here. Ellicott answers historically. Babylon was the city whose splendour dazzled and whose power destroyed Jerusalem, against whom the prophets lifted their voices as the embodiment of splendid vice and resistless power, the golden city that exalted her throne above the stars; in that greatness she became the type of later world-powers, and the power that had taken her place of pride when this was written was Rome. Yet he cautions at once that the very freedom with which the seer transfers the older prophetic language to the Rome of his day should warn us against merely local interpretations. Robertson supports the identification from a detail and at once loosens it, since Babylon drew its wealth through the Euphrates and its canals while Rome has no such system, so the image is transferred rather than described, as Nineveh and Tyre had been called harlots before. Gill, Barnes, Henry and Clarke press the identification further and read the woman as the Church of Rome, Barnes adding that the princes of Europe were under her influence through the dark ages and some remain so. Bede alone reads none of this geographically: she is the multitude of the lost who left the Creator, sitting upon the waves because the waves are the discord of the peoples, set against the believers who were of one heart and one soul.

The two acts charged in the second verse are taken separately. On the fornication, Robertson gives the political sense: the kings purchased the favour of Rome by accepting her suzerainty and with it her vices and idolatries. Barnes and Gill give it the ecclesiastical sense they have fixed on, spiritual adultery, the seduction of rulers into unfaithfulness and image-worship. Henry keeps the figure in view and presses what makes it apt: a harlot in this sense is a married woman false to her husband's bed, who has forsaken the guide of her youth and broken the covenant of God, so the charge is treachery and not merely vice. On the drunkenness they are agreed and vivid. Ellicott renders it that the dwellers on earth lost reason and self-control from the wine, and calls the draught both delicious and delirious. Barnes asks what better describes an influence leaving men incapable of sober judgment. Clarke writes that their subjects drank deep, dreadfully deep, into her errors. Wesley turns it into a maxim, that no wine can intoxicate those who drink it more thoroughly than false zeal intoxicates her followers. Bede reaches the same point by his own road: those who seek earthly things proudly are defiled by the allurement of the world and made drunk by madness of mind.
3:
Gill is careful that the carrying away was visionary, John no more removed from Patmos than Ezekiel when borne to Jerusalem in the visions of God. Why the scene is a wilderness none can say from the text, and each supplies a reason. Robertson recalls that Isaiah twice calls Babylon a desert, so the seer may be shown the city's fate, or may stand in the waste this side of her and see it. Ellicott finds the point in the contrast, the woman splendid and her surroundings desolate, and sets her against the woman clothed with the sun, driven into a wilderness and there persecuted but not forsaken; this one, amid her dazzle, is still in a wilderness. Barnes reports that Stuart took the desert as symbolising the beast's future condition, and adds his own guess from the city's state at the rise of the papal power. On the beast, Robertson observes that in the earlier vision the blasphemous names stood on the seven heads, here on the whole body; Ellicott sets it against the living creatures teeming with eyes, tokens of obedience and intelligence, where this one teems with tokens of lawlessness.

The attire is described minutely and they follow closely. Barnes explains the purple as the dye got from a Mediterranean shell-fish, worn by persons of rank, and notes it holds more blue than crimson, the words being sometimes interchanged, one Gospel calling the mock robe purple where another calls it scarlet. Ellicott makes that robe the point of the allusion, purple being what was put on our Lord in mockery, and would render the next word gilded rather than decked, the effect being one of imperial splendour like the description of Tyre. Robertson adds that the verb for gilding occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and suspects Asian temple prostitutes' finery lies behind the picture. Wesley gives the colours a civil meaning instead, purple being the imperial habit in peace and scarlet in war. Then the cup. Ellicott recalls that Jeremiah had called Babylon a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, and describes this one as full of a power that robbed men of their senses, quoting the poet's lines on the potion that changes the human countenance into some brutish form. Barnes puts it plainly, that what seemed a cup of wine was a cup of abominable drugs. Gill takes the array as expressing her grandeur and bloody disposition together; Clarke, the pomp with which her worship was held out to the nations.

The forehead name is explained from Roman manners. Robertson notes that harlots there wore a label bearing their names on their brows, citing Seneca and Juvenal; Gill cites Daubuz for the same practice, and sets the inscription against the high priest's mitre, which bore holiness to the Lord in the same place. Robertson adds the contrast that Christ has a name on his garment and the redeemed God's name on their foreheads. On the word mystery both take it as a direction to the reader. Robertson takes it to mean that Babylon is to be read mystically for Rome; Barnes objects to the printing, since nothing in the original answers to the capitals, and would render it that a name was written, a mysterious name, the mystery lying in the words Babylon and mother being symbolical, not in the thing itself. Clarke reads the public inscription as evidence that she professes her doctrines openly, having refused to be ashamed. On the drunkenness they are unsparing. Robertson observes that being drunk with blood was a common figure among the ancients and names five. Barnes traces it to the custom of drinking a slain enemy's blood in revenge. Gill says a woman drunk is shameful, but drunk with blood, and not her own, is monstrous. Wesley says he wondered exceedingly, at her cruelty and at the patience of God.
7:
The angel's question is read as kindness rather than rebuke. Barnes supposes John stood fixed in astonishment, and takes the asking why he wondered as designed to show that the cause of the surprise was about to be removed. Clarke says what there was to astonish: the woman was drunk with the blood of the saints while the beast that carried her abounded with sacred appellations, holy and most holy and most Christian; and he holds the explanation so important that without it the mystery could never have been made out. Gill notes only that this is the same angel as before, and Robertson that the interpretation now given runs to the end of the chapter. Henry makes the shrewdest remark of the four. The angel undertakes to open the vision, it being the key to the visions that went before; and yet, he says, it is so explained as still to need further explanation. That is worth carrying into what follows, since each then supplies the further explanation from a different quarter, and no two supply the same.

What the beast is that was and is not divides them completely. Robertson keeps it in the first century: the phrase answers the description of God as him who was and who is, and amounts to a parody of that name; the beast is no longer simply the empire but an emperor who died and is expected to live again, most interpreters finding here the hope of a returning Nero, realised in the emperor then reigning. Gill will have none of that, ruling out both the devil, who is distinguished from the beast, and any particular emperor such as Domitian, and takes the beast for the Roman empire itself, which carried and supported the Papacy. Clarke identifies it with the Latin kingdom: it was, since Latinus was the first of those kings; it is not, since that nation long ago ceased to be independent; and its ascent out of the pit is therefore still future. Henry keeps it functional rather than personal: it was a seat of idolatry and persecution, it is not in the ancient pagan shape, and yet it is, being truly that seat under another. Barnes reduces the clause to three assertions: that the power once was, that it had become practically extinct, and that it would so revive as to be said to stand yet. Wesley calls the description punctual and divides the duration into three periods.

On the ascent out of the abyss they agree in substance. Henry takes idolatry and cruelty to be the issue and product of hell, so that the beast comes from where it belongs and returns there; Barnes says it would seem extinct and then revive as though coming from the world over which Satan presides, and would be in its revived character such as that origin would lead one to expect; Wesley has it rise again with diabolical strength and fury but not reign long, going soon into perdition. On the wondering, Robertson marks the difference between the two amazements here: John wondered with horrible surprise, while the world will wonder and admire. Barnes takes the wonder to be general, the thing being so contrary to the regular course of events as to draw the attention of all. Clarke narrows the earth to the Latin world and turns the clause into a test, holding that those who wonder are precisely those whose names are absent from the book of life, men who prefer councils to revelation and take their religion from missals and legends, while those who abide by Scripture alone are the exception; he cites an earlier expositor for their holding this great monarchy in reverence. Gill takes the beast's variety of fortunes as the point, the empire having passed through many hands and yet remaining.
9:
The formula asking for wisdom is taken as a warning that what follows is hard. Barnes says it marks a case not to be settled by ordinary minds, and reports Stuart's rendering, that here is a meaning which comprises wisdom. Gill agrees that even after the angel's explanation much wisdom is wanted, citing the Arabic and Vulgate for renderings that make it a demand on the reader rather than a description of the vision. Ellicott turns it toward the reader's temper rather than his cleverness: it needs true wisdom to look at the world's history and not stumble. Then the seven mountains divide them at once. Robertson and Barnes take the plain reference, Rome being known to its poets as the city on seven hills, though Robertson notes the heads have shifted from the beast to the woman who rides it. Ellicott keeps Rome but widens it, holding the literal basis a vehicle for something larger, the world-city sitting among the empires that have risen like mountains through history. Wesley narrows it further, referring the hills not to ancient Rome but to those in use under the papacy. Clarke denies the reference altogether, objecting that modern Rome does not stand so, and reads mountains figuratively as seven great powers.

On the seven kings the question is what kind of thing a king is here, and the answer governs everything after. Barnes sets out the range of the word, from a literal monarch through any person of distinguished honour to a dynasty or form of administration, and says it would be contrary to the passage's spirit to insist on the narrowest sense. Ellicott takes the widest, that whole kingdoms are meant, arguing from the vocabulary: the verb used of the five is the one employed for political catastrophe, so that applying it to individual men would force it to mean merely that they died. He supports this from Daniel, whose four beasts are called kings and plainly stand for kingdoms, noting that two world-powers had preceded them. Robertson holds the opposite and keeps to men, admitting the identification is one of the puzzles of the book, that the counting is awkward because three emperors reigned too briefly to include, and that the one who must continue a short space has been taken for the emperor who died after two years. Clarke uses the same clause against that reading, arguing that since the heads are called kings as well, kingdoms cannot be what the mountains mean; he makes them seven supreme forms of Latin government.

On the eighth they are nearest in logic and furthest apart on the referent, though all see it is not an additional head. Ellicott puts it best: when the seven fall no eighth head rises, but the beast, whose vitality has shown itself through all of them, becomes as it were an eighth, not one of the seven but one out of them, so that in its death-throe the ebbing life of all finds a last expression; he observes too that the beast does not fall as the heads fall but goes into destruction. Barnes reaches the same shape, a power whose identity persists through every change and whose last form so nearly prolongs the rest that it scarcely merited separate mention. Clarke argues formally that to make a new head the form of government must differ in nature and in name, so this can only be the restoration of one of the seven. Then they part. Robertson takes the eighth for the emperor reigning as John wrote, reckoned among the seven because men thought him a second Nero, and notes that his assassination was itself a symbol of the end toward which the beast hastened. Gill and Clarke take it for a power still to come, Gill naming the Papacy as the only surviving head of a Roman empire become Papal.
12:
The horns are distinguished from the heads, and the distinction is pressed. Robertson keeps the two apart, the heads being emperors and the horns kings, and notes the comparative particle: they are like kings rather than the emperors themselves, succeeding them with something short of imperial power. Ellicott, consistent with his reading of the heads, will not have them personal sovereigns but kingdoms or nationalities whose hour arrives only when the sixth head falls. Barnes agrees they are kingdoms not yet in existence when this was written, and takes the hour as marking something brief and provisional, which he finds exactly true of the governments thrown up after the northern invasions. Clarke translates it one time rather than one hour, so their reign is concurrent with the beast's and not merely short. Gill is most concrete. He rejects the reckoning that makes them Christian emperors from Constantine to Theodosius, since those never gave their kingdoms to the beast, and rejects equally the reading that postpones them to the end of the world; he takes them for the kingdoms into which the empire broke when the Goths and Vandals tore it, identifies them with the ten toes of the image and the ten horns of Daniel's fourth beast, and notes that interpreters count them differently.

The one mind is read by each in his own key. Robertson takes it simply as one purpose, and observes the symmetry: as the dragon gave power and authority to the beast, so these are wholly at the beast's service. Ellicott makes the observation that carries furthest: though sundered powers, they are one in their subjection, and the point survives the empire that suggested it, since the idea of a universal empire may disappear while the spirit of mere earthliness remains, needing no power the size of Rome to illustrate it. Gill and Barnes take the unity to be religious rather than political, and narrate it as history. Gill says the princes and their subjects came in time to one religion, first Arian, then Papist. Barnes says the same at more length: kingdoms of different origin, often at war with one another, all became Roman Catholic and upheld the Papacy; most of their peoples were at first pagan; many embraced Christianity in its Arian form, which for a time was a bar; and he dates the turn from the conversion of Clovis. Clarke keeps to his own scheme, making the ten the strength of the Latin empire, monarchs independent of each other in all but implicit obedience to the Latin Church.

Henry sets the scene as a contrast between appearances and outcome. To an eye of sense the beast and his army are far the stronger, and one would think an army with a Lamb at its head could not stand before the great red dragon; yet the Lamb overcomes, Christ reigning till all enemies are under his feet. He grounds the victory twice over, on the Lamb's title, having supreme dominion by nature and by office, and on the character of the followers, called out by commission, chosen and fitted for the warfare, faithful in it, so that such an army under such a commander will at length carry all before it. Robertson notes the title is given to Christ again later and to God in the Law and the Prophets, and infers that crowned heads are Christ's subjects; those with him shall also overcome, sharing the triumph as they shared the conflict. Gill denies a personal or final battle is meant and refers the war to the persecution of Christ's members in every age; Clarke and Barnes agree, Barnes adding that it is waged not by open proclamation but by sustaining a persecuting power. Ellicott asks when the war is made and answers morally, not by date: whenever the policy of nations favours oppression and worldliness, they are not with Christ but against him.
15:
The waters are interpreted for us, and each follows the figure out. Robertson notes the Old Testament had long used waters for peoples, and quotes the judgment that Rome's danger lay in the multitudes under her sway. Barnes takes outspread seas and raging floods as the natural emblem of such numbers, and adds that the four terms mark diversity as well as multitude, so that perhaps no government before, neither Babylonian nor Macedonian nor Roman, had gathered so many peoples of so many tongues. Clarke turns the plurals into a polemical point by way of Bishop Newton: the Church which sits on these waters glories in the title Catholic and counts the number and variety of her adherents as itself a proof of the true religion, one controversialist making her very name his first note of the Church. Ellicott alone draws a moral from the image rather than an identification. Both beast and harlot draw much of their power from the people, since the easily-moved passions of a crowd are what subtle and seductive enemies use; and he quotes the saying that men never so much need to be theocratic as when they are most democratic, a newly discovered strength being what unscrupulous ambition makes a tool of.

The turn of the horns against the woman surprises them. Barnes says so outright: there seems an incongruity, since these powers were lately in alliance with the beast and gave it all their strength, so what is said here must belong to a later period and mark a great change of policy. He then reads his own century into it, France having struck heavy blows and England having been detached. Clarke finds here a clue to the whole question of the horns: since they are to hate her and be reformed from her, no power that had ceased before the Reformation can be one of them, so the ten must be the great European states standing at its commencement. Ellicott keeps to the picture: she was seen in splendid apparel riding the beast, and now the beast turns his horns upon her, leaves her deserted, strips her ornaments, consumes the spoil, which is what eating her flesh means, and burns her; other kingdoms rise who hate her tyranny and covet her wealth, and she falls like Jezebel. Robertson dates it in history, noting that John wrote before Alaric and Genseric and the hordes that devastated Rome, and that no reader of Gibbon will want for illustrations.

That God put it in their hearts governs the whole, and none softens it. Gill distinguishes three senses of the divine will, approving, commanding and determining, and says the time of her reign is fixed, so these kings do not so much their own will as God's, who holds their hearts and turns them as rivers of water. Henry puts it more starkly, that God so ruled them by his providence that they did, without intending it, the very thing he had purposed; and he adds what they will feel afterwards, that they shall see their folly and how they were bewitched by her, their joining in sin turning at last to hatred and rage. Robertson calls the clause a plain statement of God's over-ruling hand among the nations, and Ellicott sums it: thus does the wrath of man ever turn to God's praise. Clarke warns against thinking such kingdoms rise by human power or the chances of war, and bids the nations tremble when a wicked monarchy rises, since it is raised to execute vengeance. On the last verse they agree the woman is a city and that Rome is meant, Barnes noting that expositors differ only over whether it is Rome pagan or Christian, and Clarke insisting a city is the plainer emblem of a Church. Robertson leaves the door open: Rome followed Babylon, and other cities may follow in their train.
